title: Option (instead of null)
intro: Rust has no nil or null. A value that might be missing has the type `Option<T>`, which is either `Some(value)` or `None`.

coming_from.go: `Option<User>` replaces a `*User` that might be nil, and also the `(value, ok)` pair from a map lookup: one value carries both. You can't reach `.name` until you've checked for `Some`, so you can't dereference a missing value by accident.
coming_from.kotlin: `Option<User>` is your `User?`, and for Kotlin code the compiler checks it just as strictly. The operators become methods: `?.` is `.map(...)` or `.and_then(...)`, `?:` is `.unwrap_or_else(...)` (both are lazy), and `!!` is `.unwrap()`. `Option` is an ordinary type rather than a mark on a type, so it nests (`Option<Option<T>>`) and has methods, and no value arrives from Java with unknown nullness.
coming_from.python: `Option<User>` is your `Optional[User]`, but the check isn't left to a tool you may forget to run: the compiler won't let you touch `.name` until you've matched `Some`. That removes the unchecked AttributeError on `None`.
coming_from.typescript: `Option<User>` is `User | undefined` with `strictNullChecks` always on. Rust has one "nothing", `None`, not both `null` and `undefined`. There is no `?.` or `??`: you use methods like `.map(...)` and `.unwrap_or(...)`, or `match` and `if let`.
coming_from.java: `Option<T>` is `Optional<T>`, but in Rust it is the standard way to say a value may be missing, and there is no `null` for an `Option` itself to be. Java still has `null` for every reference, including an `Optional` variable. `match` or `if let` do what `ifPresentOrElse` and `map(...).orElse(...)` do.
coming_from.csharp: `Option<User>` is what `User?` means, but Rust enforces it: you cannot touch `.name` until you've checked for `Some`. With nullable reference types, C# reports the same mistake (CS8602) as a warning by default, and the program still builds.
coming_from.c: `Option<&User>` replaces a pointer that might be `NULL`, and it is stored as just that pointer, with `None` as the null address. The difference is that you must check for `None` before using it; you can't forget and read address 0.
coming_from.cpp: `Option<T>` is `std::optional<T>`. `if (auto u = f())` tests the optional, but `u` is still an optional and `u->name` skips the test; Rust has no such shortcut, and `unwrap()` panics with a message on `None` instead of being undefined behaviour. `Option<&T>` is what `std::optional<T&>` is in C++26, and what a raw pointer was before.

notes: `Option<User>` is either `Some(user)` or `None`. In safe Rust a reference is never null, so "might be missing" is spelled out as a type you can see.

Handy shortcuts: `opt.unwrap_or(default)` gives a fallback value, `opt.map(|u| u.name)` changes the value inside if there is one (`|u| u.name` is a closure, a small function written inline; [Closures](/learn/closures/) come later), and `opt?` inside a function that returns Option hands back None early.
`opt.unwrap()` takes the value out and crashes if it is None. Use it only where None really cannot happen.
Missing for a reason, not by accident: if a function can fail with a reason, return a `Result` instead (next lesson). `Option` says "nothing"; `Result` says why.

gotcha.title: Using the value without checking
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `u := findUser(2); fmt.Println(u.Name)` compiles fine. At runtime `u` is nil, and the program crashes with a nil pointer dereference. Kotlin refuses at compile time, like Rust.
gotcha.rust_sees: `u` is an `Option<User>`, not a `User`. An Option has no `name` field. You have to open it first.
gotcha.why: Rust moves the nil check from "remember to do it" to "can't compile without it". Every place that might get nothing has to say what happens then. The compiler's `help:` suggests `u.unwrap().name`. That compiles, but `unwrap` on None crashes, which is the classic null crash all over again. Use `match` or `if let` instead.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too: `findUser` returns `User?`, so `u.name` needs `u?.name` or a null check first.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:8:14: error: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'User?'.
    println(u.name)
             ^

python.says: Python runs until `u.name`, then raises AttributeError because `u` is None. This is the same crash as `None.name` anywhere. A type checker such as mypy or pyright flags it first, but only if you run one, and `# type: ignore`, `cast` and `Any` can switch the check off.
python.out:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 14, in <module>
    print(u.name)
          ^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'name'

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses this too with `strict` on: `u` is possibly `undefined`, so you must check it before reading `u.name`.

java.says: It compiles, then throws a NullPointerException because `findUser(2)` returned null. Nothing made you check first.
